<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent breakthroughs in large language model-driven <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">autonomous agents</span> have revealed that <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">multi-agent collaboration</span> often surpasses each individual through collective reasoning.
Inspired by the neural scaling law—increasing neurons enhances performance, this study explores whether the continuous addition of collaborative agents can yield similar benefits.
Technically, we utilize directed acyclic graphs to organize agents into a <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">m</span>ulti-agent <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">c</span>ollaboration <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">net</span>work (<span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>), upon which their interactive reasoning is topologically orchestrated for autonomous task solving.
Extensive evaluations reveal that it effectively supports collaboration among over a thousand agents, with irregular topologies outperforming regular ones.
We also identify a <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling law</span>—the overall performance follows a logistic growth pattern as agents scale, with collaborative emergence occurring earlier than traditional neural emergence.
We speculate this may be because scaling agents catalyzes their multidimensional considerations during interactive reflection and refinement, thereby producing more comprehensive artifacts. The code is available at <a href="https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/macnet" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/macnet</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2406.07155v3/network.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:439/180;" width="439" height="180" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Multi-agent collaboration network (<span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>) uses directed acyclic graphs to arrange agents for collaborative interactions, facilitating autonomous task-solving through collective reasoning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the rapidly advancing field of artificial intelligence, <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">large language models</span> (LLMs) have driven transformative shifts across numerous domains due to their remarkable linguistic capacity to seamlessly integrate extensive world knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Central to this breakthrough is the <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">neural scaling law</span>, where well-trained neural networks often exhibit power-law scaling relations primarily with the number of neurons, alongside factors such as dataset size and training time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Despite this, LLMs have inherent limitations in their enclosed reasoning, particularly when addressing complex situations that extend beyond textual boundaries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
To this end, during the inference phase, pioneering studies transform foundational LLMs into versatile <span id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">autonomous agents</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Richards, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2023</a>)</cite> by encapsulating external capabilities like context-aware memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, tool use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, and procedural planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
In this context, <span id="S1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">multi-agent collaboration</span>, within an interactive environment, prompts agents to engage in iterative reflection and refinement, explicitly facilitating a process of "slow thinking" <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Daniel, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite>. This paradigm effectively unites the distinct expertise of diverse agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, ultimately leading to artifacts<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          Artifacts can vary from multiple-choice answers to repository-level code or coherent narratives, among many other possibilities.</span></span></span> derived from their dialogues.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although numerous studies have confirmed that task-oriented multi-agent collaboration, facilitated by interactive behaviors, often surpasses standalone intelligence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024d</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, the potential for continuously increasing agents remains largely overlooked—with most research involving fewer than ten agents and only a limited number extending to several dozen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Inspired by the neural scaling law, a thought-provoking question arises: <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how does the continuous addition of collaborative agents impact performance?</span>
Exploring the <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling law</span> is essential for linking performance trends with inference resources, revealing underlying phenomena in agent networking, and promoting the development of scalable and predictable LLM systems.
However, technically, effective collaboration should not depend on simple majority voting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>; instead, it should incorporate strategic mechanisms for scalable networking, cooperative interaction, and progressive decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hopfield, 1982</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Almaatouq et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Toward this end, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we organize multiple agents into a <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">m</span>ulti-<span id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">a</span>gent <span id="S1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">c</span>ollaboration <span id="S1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">net</span>work (<span id="S1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>), upon which their interactive reasoning is topologically orchestrated for autonomous task solving.</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For network construction, agents’ topology is constructed as a directed acyclic graph, with each edge managed by a supervisory <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">critic</span> issuing commands, and each node by a compliant <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">actor</span> providing tailored artifacts. This establishes a functional bipartition of labor among agents, promoting role specialization while inherently preventing backflow in information propagation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:2.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S1.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For interactive reasoning, agents interact in a topological order, where each round involves two adjacent agents refining a previous artifact, and only the refined artifact, rather than the entire dialogue, is propagated to the next rounds.
This prevents global broadcasting and suppresses context explosion, thereby enhancing collaboration scalability for much larger networks.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We performed extensive evaluations across different downstream scenarios, employing three types of representative topologies—chain, tree, and graph—further divided into six representative variants.
The results show that <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span> surpasses all baselines on average and supports effective collaboration among over a thousand agents.
Counterintuitively, collaborating within irregular topologies unexpectedly outperforms that within regular ones.
Notably, we reveal a <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling law</span>, indicating that the overall performance exhibits a logistic growth pattern as the process of scaling agents, with collaborative emergence occurring earlier than previous instances of neural emergence.
We speculate this may be because scaling agents catalyzes their multidimensional considerations during interactive reflection and refinement, thereby producing more comprehensive artifacts.
Longer term, we aim for this research to extrapolate the traditional scaling from training to inference, circumventing the need for resource-intensive retraining through inference-time procedural thinking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Multi-Agent Collaboration Network</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To create a scalable environment for effective collaboration, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we organize multiple agents into a <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">m</span>ulti-<span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">a</span>gent <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">c</span>ollaboration <span id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uwave">net</span>work (<span id="S2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>), upon which their interactive reasoning is topologically orchestrated for autonomous task solving.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Network Construction</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although training-time neuron collaboration has been well-established with Transformer architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, the suitable architectures for inference-time agent collaboration remain unclear and lack consensus.
Toward this end, we draw on the concept of graphs—a data structure that describes entities and their interrelations—and extend from previous efforts to propose a more general topology as a <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">directed acyclic graph</span> (DAG) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsson et al., 2020</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})\quad\mathcal{V}=\{v_{i}|i\in I\}\quad\mathcal{E}=\{\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle|i,j\in I\wedge i\neq j\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>∧</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})\quad\mathcal{V}=\{v_{i}|i\in I\}\quad\mathcal{E}=\{\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle|i,j\in I\wedge i\neq j\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of nodes indexed by the index set <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of edges, with each edge directed from one node to another and no cycles exist.
A graph will orchestrate agent interactions, akin to social networks where information propagates through directed edges.
Intuitively, the acyclic nature prevents information backflow, eliminating the need for additional designs like task-specific cycle-breaking, thereby enhancing generalizability and adaptability across contexts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:186.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2406.07155v3/graph.svg" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:258/163;" width="258" height="163"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Representative topologies.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:186.8pt;"><img src="2406.07155v3/graph_agentization.png" id="S2.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:258/150;" width="258" height="150" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Assign functionally bipartite agents on nodes and edges, respectively.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given the impracticality of enumerating all possible topologies, we focus on three prevalent types—chain, tree, and graph—further divided into six representative sub-topologies, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Network Construction ‣ 2 Multi-Agent Collaboration Network ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
Chain topologies, resembling the waterfall model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Petersen et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, linearly structuring interactions along agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Tree topologies enable agents to branch out, interacting in independent directions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib106" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>; further categorized into "wider" star-shaped and "deeper" tree-shaped topologies.
Graph topologies support arbitrary interaction dependencies, with nodes having multiple children and parents, forming either divergent or convergent interactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Besta et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024d</a>; <a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuge et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; further classified into fully-connected mesh topologies, MLP-shaped layered topologies, and irregular random topologies.
These representative topologies are extensively studied in complex network <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dodds et al., 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Newman, 2001</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and procedural reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Besta et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, ensuring a comprehensive coverage of the most widespread and practical topologies in multi-agent networking.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since a functional bipartition—consisting of supervisory critics who issue directional instructions and compliant actors who provide tailored artifacts—can effectively establish division of labor, activate functional behaviors, and facilitate progressive task-solving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Network Construction ‣ 2 Multi-Agent Collaboration Network ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we strategically assign a critic to each edge and an actor to each node:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{i}}=\rho(v_{i}),\ \forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}\quad\bm{a_{ij}}=\rho(\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle),\ \forall\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>∀</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{i}}=\rho(v_{i}),\ \forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}\quad\bm{a_{ij}}=\rho(\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle),\ \forall\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(x)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the <span id="S2.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">agentization</span> operation on an element <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, achieved by equipping a foundation model with context-aware memory, external tools, and professional roles; <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{ij}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{ij}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote an actor assigned to node <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and a critic assigned to edge <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Interactive Reasoning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In procedural task-solving, interactive reasoning among agents within a static network requires strategical traversal to establish an orderly interaction criterion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024e</a>)</cite>.
In a directed acyclic setting, our graph traversal strategy adheres to the principles of <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">topological ordering</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kahn, 1962</a>)</cite>, which ensures that each node is visited only after all its dependencies have been traversed.
Formally, for a network <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, its topological order is a linear arrangement of agents <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{ij}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{ij}}</annotation></semantics></math> such that for every directed edge <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>, the ordering satisfies:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E},\ \mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{i}})&lt;\mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{ij}})&lt;\mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{j}})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>∀</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle\in\mathcal{E},\ \mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{i}})&lt;\mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{ij}})&lt;\mathbb{I}(\bm{a_{j}})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{I}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{I}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the index of agent <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in a topological sequence. This arrangement ensures that each node-occupied agent <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> precedes its corresponding edge-occupied agent <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{ij}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{ij}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{ij}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{ij}}</annotation></semantics></math> precedes <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math>, thereby ensuring orderly information propogation along the network.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2406.07155v3/dynamics.png" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:543/99;" width="543" height="99" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Orchestrating the agents’ reasoning process involves a series of dual-agent interactions. The topological order serves as the control flow, while the original connectivity governs the data flow.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After establishing the global order, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.2 Interactive Reasoning ‣ 2 Multi-Agent Collaboration Network ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we enable each pair of edge-connected adjacent agents to interact for artifact refinement, which results in a total assignment of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{V}|+|\mathcal{E}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{V}|+|\mathcal{E}|</annotation></semantics></math> agents and require at least <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times|\mathcal{E}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times|\mathcal{E}|</annotation></semantics></math> interaction rounds. Specifically, within each edge, the interactions between critics and actors follows a dual-agent multi-turn pattern:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}},\bm{a_{j}})=\big(\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}}),\tau(\bm{a_{ij}},\bm{a_{j}})\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathsize="1.200em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}},\bm{a_{j}})=\big(\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}}),\tau(\bm{a_{ij}},\bm{a_{j}})\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E4Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}})=(\bm{a_{i}}\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tau(\bm{a_{i},\bm{a_{ij}}})=(\bm{a_{i}}\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bm{a_{ij}},\ \bm{a_{ij}}\leadsto\bm{a_{i}})_{\circlearrowleft}\quad\tau(\bm{a_{ij}},\bm{a_{j}})=(\bm{a_{ij}}\rightarrow\bm{a_{j}},\ \bm{a_{j}}\leadsto\bm{a_{ij}})_{\circlearrowleft}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">↝</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mo>↺</mo></msub><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.667em">,</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">↝</mo><mi>𝒂</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mo>↺</mo></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bm{a_{ij}},\ \bm{a_{ij}}\leadsto\bm{a_{i}})_{\circlearrowleft}\quad\tau(\bm{a_{ij}},\bm{a_{j}})=(\bm{a_{ij}}\rightarrow\bm{a_{j}},\ \bm{a_{j}}\leadsto\bm{a_{ij}})_{\circlearrowleft}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the interaction between agents, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> signifies an act of requesting, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leadsto" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↝</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leadsto</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a corresponding reply—within which the critic provides an instruction and the actor offers an artifact, and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\circlearrowleft" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>↺</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\circlearrowleft</annotation></semantics></math> denotes an iterative process.
That is, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒊</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> requests feedback, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{ij}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mrow><mi>𝒊</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝒋</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{ij}}</annotation></semantics></math> offers reflected suggestions and requests further refinement, and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{a_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒂</mi><mi>𝒋</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{a_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math> provides a refined artifact.
Thus, the agents associated with a single edge can engage in iterative reflection and refinement, effectively implementing an refinement of a previous artifact <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Renze &amp; Guven, 2024</a>)</cite>.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            Note that although the interaction order is unfolded as a sequence for visualization purposes only, certain sub-topologies (<span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g., </span>star) inherently support parallel processing.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Memory Control</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Note that unrestrained information exchange among agents inevitably leads to <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">context explosion</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, ultimately hindering scalability by limiting support for additional entities.
To address this, we adopt both short- and long-term memory to manage the context visibility for each agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sumers et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Short-term memory</span> captures the working memory within each interaction, ensuring context-aware decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Long-term memory</span> maintains context continuity by retaining only the final artifact derived from current dialogue, rather than the entire conversational history, ensuring that non-artifact contexts (<span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g., </span>the detailed analysis process preceding an artifact) remain inaccessible<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            Inaccessibility doesn’t mean abandonment; when agents incorporate previous contexts into an artifact, these contexts are implicitly embedded and carried forward with the artifact.</span></span></span> to subsequent agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>.
This mechanism ensures that only the artifact propagates through the network, which explicitly minimizes context explosion risk while maintaining continuity.
Artifacts propagate by branching at divergent nodes, or merging at convergent nodes requiring effective aggregation; technically, before refinement, convergent agents integrate the strengths of incoming artifacts through hierarchical aggregation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> to yield a "non-linearly" strength-aggregated artifact.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Theoretically, in a mesh structure characterized by the highest interaction density, the total token consumption for the sink<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
            The ”sink agent” refers to the agent assigned to the sink node. In a multi-sink structure, a final sink node is automatically appended to form a structure with only one sink.</span></span></span> agent who experiences maximum context pressure, with and without this mechanism, is derived as follows:</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E5X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(n)_{\text{w/o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext>w/o</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(n)_{\text{w/o}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=t+p+s+(2m-1)(i+s)(n(n-1)/2+2(n-2))\overset{n\gg 1}{\approx}Cn^{2}\propto n^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">≫</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">1</mn></mrow></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=t+p+s+(2m-1)(i+s)(n(n-1)/2+2(n-2))\overset{n\gg 1}{\approx}Cn^{2}\propto n^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="3" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E5Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(n)_{\text{w/}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext>w/</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(n)_{\text{w/}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=t+p+s+m(i+s)((n-1)+2(n-2))\overset{n\gg 1}{\approx}\bar{C}n\propto n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">≫</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">1</mn></mrow></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=t+p+s+m(i+s)((n-1)+2(n-2))\overset{n\gg 1}{\approx}\bar{C}n\propto n</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E5Xb" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5Xb.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{where}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtext>where</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{where}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5Xb.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle C\equiv(2m-1)(i+s)/2\quad\bar{C}\equiv 3m(i+s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>C</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle C\equiv(2m-1)(i+s)/2\quad\bar{C}\equiv 3m(i+s)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the network scale (<span id="S2.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e., <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{V}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{V}|</annotation></semantics></math></span>), <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> the task length, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> the profile length, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> the average instruction length, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> the average artifact length, and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> the maximum interaction rounds between adjacent agents.
This token complexity analysis implies that, without memory control, context length grows with <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, causing squared increases in time and cost as the network scales.
Conversely, our mechanism decouples context length from quadratic to linear growth, effectively suppressing context explosion and enabling better scalability for larger networks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We select a diverse set of representative methods to facilitate a comprehensive multidimensional comparison:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CoT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022b</a>)</cite> is a technically general and empirically powerful approach that endows LLMs with the ability to generate a coherent series of intermediate reasoning steps, naturally leading to the final artifact through process-aware thoughtful thinking.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AutoGPT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Richards, 2023</a>)</cite> is a versatile agent that employs multi-step planning and tool-augmented reasoning to decompose complex tasks into chained subtasks and leverages external tools within an environment-feedback cycle to progressively develop effective artifacts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">GPTSwarm</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuge et al., 2024</a>)</cite> formalizes a swarm of autonomous agents as computational graphs, with nodes as manually-customized functions and edges facilitating information flow, adaptively optimizing node prompts and modifying graph connectivity during collective reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I1.i4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AgentVerse</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024d</a>)</cite> dynamically assembles and coordinates a team of expert agents in chained or hierarchical structures, employing multi-agent linguistic interaction to autonomously reflect and refine artifacts while displaying emergent social behaviors.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets and Metrics</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt publicly available and logically challenging benchmarks to evaluate performance across heterogeneous downstream scenarios.</p>
<ol id="S3.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> provides a comprehensive set of logical reasoning assessments across diverse subjects and difficulties, utilizing multiple-option questions to measure general world knowledge and logical inference capabilities. We assess the quality of generated artifacts via <span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">accuracy</span>, which reflects the correctness of responses to multiple-choice questions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, a widely recognized benchmark for function-level code generation, designed for measuring basic programming skills. We assess via <span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">pass@k</span>, which reflects function correctness across multiple standard test cases.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SRDD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024c</a>)</cite> integrates complex textual software requirements from major real-world application platforms, tailored for repository-level software development, involving requirement comprehension, system design, code generation and testing. We assess using the official comprehensive metric encompassing completeness, executability, and consistency.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><math id="S3.I2.i4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bullet" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bullet</annotation></semantics></math></span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CommonGen-Hard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>)</cite> tests the ability to generate coherent sentences with discrete concepts, assessing contextual understanding, commonsense reasoning, and creative writing skills. We assess using a comprehensive metric that integrates crucial factors including grammar, fluency, context relevance, and logic consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation Details</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct non-deterministic topologies such as trees and graphs utilizing fundamental structures, including binary trees, layered structures balanced in both width and depth, and random structures crafted by removing edges from a mesh while maintaining connectivity.
By default, we employ a topology consisting of approximately four nodes, aligning with multi-agent baselines.
GPT-3.5 is employed for interactive reasoning due to its optimal balance of efficacy and efficiency, with each iterative interaction limited to three exchange rounds.</p>
</div>
