A dagger (<math id="S3.T1.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math>) denotes statistically significant differences (<math id="S3.T1.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\leq 0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\leq 0.05</annotation></semantics></math>) between a method and our chain-structured setting.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Does Our Method Lead to Improved Performance?</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ the simplest topology—chain—as the default setting for comparative analysis. As demonstrated in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Implementation Details ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the chain-structured method consistently surpasses all baselines across most metrics, showing a significant margin of improvement.
The primary advantage of <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet-Chain</span>, over a single agent who provides artifacts directly, lies in its facilitation of a procedural thinking in which artifacts are continually reflected and refined. This process effectively mitigates previous inaccuracies or unexpected hallucinations, aligning with previous findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, we observe that <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CoT</span> exhibits strong performance on certain datasets, which is largely because the underlying knowledge of widely-researched benchmarks is already embedded in foundational models, giving single agents a notable capability in these relatively "simple" tasks.
While <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">GPTSwarm</span> self-organizes agents through dynamic optimization of nodes and edges, it necessitates extensive task-specific customization for all nodes and edges, complicating usage and thus hindering seamless generalization to heterogeneous downstream tasks.
Given the growing need for highly performant and automatic real-world systems, it is impractical to expect that all preparatory knowledge can be fully pre-encoded in foundation models, nor can specific adaptations be pre-made for all unforeseen complex tasks.
Fortunately, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span> bridges this gap by automatically generating various networks through simple hyperparameters (<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g., </span>topology type and scale), enabling agents to engage in cooperative interactions without needing specific adjustments<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            Experiments with open-source models demonstrate a similar pattern.</span></span></span>, which represents a promising pathway to achieving both autonomy and generalizability.
Furthermore, we simulate a regression to graph-of-thought reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Besta et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> with a simplified agent by ablating agents’ profiles, which led to an average performance drop of 3.67% across all topologies. This result underscores the effectiveness of collective intelligence over singular-aspect reasoning, as the latter represents a variant of dimensionality reduction within multi-agent environments, inevitably blocking its potential to extrapolate potential opportunities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>How Do Different Topologies Perform Against Each Other?</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To gain a deeper understanding of the impact on organizational structures within multi-agent collaboration, we examine <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>’s topologies across six representative topologies. The analysis focuses on three key perspectives: density, shape, and direction.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Density Perspective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Implementation Details ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates that different types of topologies vary significantly in effectiveness for specific tasks; no single topology consistently excels across all tasks.
For instance, a chain topology is more suitable for software development, while a tree topology is ideal for creative writing.
This phenomenon may arise from the inherent suitability of software engineering to a linear process, which is accomplished through sequential steps such as analysis, coding, review, and testing; in contrast, tasks requiring high creativity necessitate more divergent structures to foster agent interactions from various aspects.
Additionally, higher interaction density, associated with edge density (see Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Shape Perspective ‣ 3.2 How Do Different Topologies Perform Against Each Other? ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), correlates with improved average performance across the three primary topological types.
Specifically, the densely connected mesh topology outperforms the moderately dense tree topology, which in turn outperforms the sparsely connected chain topology.
This can be attributed to the fact that increased density natually prolongs the reasoning process among collective agents, potentially enhancing opportunities for optimizing artifacts from various aspects.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Shape Perspective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the intuitive appeal of densest interactions (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e., </span>mesh), they do not always yield optimal performance. In contrast, irregular topologies often demonstrate statistically significant advantages.
We hypothesize that this phenomenon is because overly dense interactions can overwhelm agents with information overload, impeding effective reflection and refinement. Conversely, network randomization frequently induces small-world properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Watts &amp; Strogatz, 1998</a>)</cite>, characterized by a shorter <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">average path length<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">6</span></span>
                  
                  
                  
                <span id="footnote6.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">Average path length </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="footnote6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">(</span><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Albert &amp; Barabasi, 2002</a><span id="footnote6.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">)</span></cite><span id="footnote6.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is the average number of steps along the shortest paths for all possible pairs of network nodes, which is a measure of the efficiency of information transport on a network.</span></span></span></span></span> or a higher <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">clustering coefficient<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">7</span></span>
                  
                  
                  
                <span id="footnote7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">The clustering coefficient measures the connectivity density among a node’s neighbors </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><span id="footnote7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">(</span><a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Strogatz, 2001</a><span id="footnote7.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">)</span></cite><span id="footnote7.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">.</span></span></span></span></span>.
These random edge connections, akin to residual connections, can link "unacquainted" agents via direct shortcuts, transforming them into "acquaintances" and implicitly reducing the average path length, which naturally decreases the likelihood of long-distance artifact invisibility.
This phenomenon, seemingly counterintuitive when compared to well-established regular organizational structures in the real world, suggests that collaboration patterns in an agent’s world need not precisely mirror those in human society.
Additionally, random topologies consume approximately 51.92% less time than mesh topologies, striking an optimal balance between reduced density and enhanced efficiency, thus serving as a more practical choice.
It has also been noticed that, with the same density, star-shaped topologies that are "wider" tend to perform better than "deeper" tree-shaped ones.
This is primarily due to the memory control mechanism; while it efficiently manages the spread of overly lengthy contexts across the network, it may cause deeper topologies to lose track of distant agents, occasionally resulting in artifact version rollbacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
This points to an empirical search strategy that manages network scale and clustering coefficients, whether through automated searching or manual design, to find an optimal balance between effectiveness and efficiency.
Delving deeper, an in-depth inductive bias analysis reveals that in closed-domain scenarios (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g., </span>logical choices), a chain structure significantly aids in facilitating step-by-step reasoning. Conversely, a proliferation of parallel branches (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g., </span>stars) can lead to convoluted brainstorming, which may not always be advantageous.
In open-domain scenarios, topologies characterized by more convergent nodes are shown to revise artifacts more frequently and produce longer artifacts<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
                
                
                
              The layer topologies exhibit a 92.16% modification probability and an average artifact length of 586.57, compared to 68.48% and 308.26 for chain topologies</span></span></span>.
This occurs because more convergent nodes, with increased input diversity, increase the likelihood of refining artifacts, benefiting length-sensitive metrics as longer artifacts are more likely to meet rich requirements.
Ultimately, no task is confined to a particular topology; the optimal configuration should be chosen based on the openness of scenarios, available computing resources, and associated reasoning costs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F6.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:218.6pt;"><img src="2406.07155v3/density.png" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:296/141;" width="296" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Density of different topologies at different scales.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F6.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:166.9pt;"><img src="2406.07155v3/reverse.png" id="S3.F6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:199/141;" width="199" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Comparison between topologies and their reversed counterparts.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Direction Perspective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond density and shape perspectives, the inherent asymmetry in certain topologies—where reversing the edges results in a topologically distinct configuration—has interested us in exploring the effects of reversed topologies.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Shape Perspective ‣ 3.2 How Do Different Topologies Perform Against Each Other? ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, merely reversing the directions of specific topologies can lead to significant performance degradation.
Typically, divergent topologies, characterized by having more child nodes than parent nodes, substantially outperform their convergent counterparts.
Intuitively, artifact propagation diverges smoothly, enabling each agent to discuss artifacts from varied aspects.
In contrast, aggregating multiple artifacts at a convergent node is more challenging, highlighting the complexity of integrating diverse aspects into a cohesive artifact.
Therefore, to minimize potential degradation during artifact aggregation, it is recommended to employ topologies that maximize divergence while minimizing convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Could A Collaborative Scaling Law Be Observed?</h3>

<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2406.07155v3/scaling.png" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:543/206;" width="543" height="206" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Scaling performance of multi-agent collaboration under different topologies. Quality represents the average performance over all tasks.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Trend Perspective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recall the neural scaling law, which posits that increasing neurons leads to an continual performance improvement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
To investigate the <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling law</span>, which excavates the relationship between agent scale and performance, we initiated an attempt by exponentially increasing the number of nodes (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{V}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{V}|</annotation></semantics></math>) from <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (regressing to a single-agent variant) to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{6}</annotation></semantics></math> (equating to over a thousand agents in a mesh network).
As depicted in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.3 Could A Collaborative Scaling Law Be Observed? ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, scaling our networks initially grows slowly in the quality of artifacts generated by various multi-agent systems, then leads to a rapid improvement before reaching a saturation point.
This pattern resembles a sigmoid-variant function:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(|\mathcal{V}|)=\frac{\gamma}{1+e^{-\beta(\log|\mathcal{V}|-\alpha)}}+\delta" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>γ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(|\mathcal{V}|)=\frac{\gamma}{1+e^{-\beta(\log|\mathcal{V}|-\alpha)}}+\delta</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\}</annotation></semantics></math> are real numbers specific to a particular topology.
Roughly speaking, a node magnitude of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> appears to be a reasonable choice.
However, considering the efficiency of sparse topologies and the superior performance of dense ones, we advocate balancing shape and scale through multidimensional trade-offs when applying this trend to various downstream applications.
This finding suggests that many existing agent systems may be operating below their full potential, which underscores a promising path for enhancing performance by increasing the number of agents, provided they collaborate effectively, rather than solely focusing on scaling foundational models.<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
                
                
                
              Looking further, this fitting only reflects a general pattern from the perspective of network scales; future research should aim for a more precise characterization by incorporating additional factors like profiles, tools and communication protocols, or social routing.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Besides, the validation of baseline scaling reveals that equalizing the number of LLM calls—whether through majority voting in closed-domain tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> or best-of-N in open-domain tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sessa et al., 2024</a>)</cite>—consistently highlights a lack of effective scalability across all baselines.
Majority voting enhances performance by merely 0.9%, even when augmented with <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">CoT</span> or <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AutoGPT</span>, plateauing at approximately eight agents.
<span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">AgentVerse</span> implicitly reduces to a star topology and frequently encounters context explosion issues when scaling beyond thirty agents, thus hindering scalability.
The energy-intensive setup of <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">GPTSwarm</span> necessitates manual, task-specific structuring and prompting, which restricts both multitasking capabilities and overall scalability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Timing Perspective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The neural scaling law requires models with at least a billion parameters and over <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{22}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>22</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{22}</annotation></semantics></math> training FLOPs to show emergent trends <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schaeffer et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
In contrast, collaborative emergence in <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span> manifests at much smaller scales, with most topologies reaching performance saturation with approximately a hundred agents.
The fundamental reason is that neuron coordination (during training) relies on numeric matrix operations, requiring all neurons to precisely and simultaneously learn from scratch to assimilate extensive world knowledge.
Conversely, individual agents (during inference) already possess certain knowledge from the foundational models, and their coordination through interdependent interactions utilizes existing reasoning skills to disseminate knowledge from diverse aspects; the most critical aspects for artifact refinement in agents’ interactions typically do not require such a large scale to be thoroughly reflected and refined.
Thus, alongside neuron collaboration, agent collaboration may serve as a “shortcut” to enhance intelligence levels, especially when large-scale retraining resources such as data and hardware are constrained.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>What Factors Might Contribute to Collaborative Emergence?</h3>

<figure id="S3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2406.07155v3/analysis.png" id="S3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:543/155;" width="543" height="155" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>The number and distribution of aspects in agent interactions, along with the length of artifacts. The pie chart features primary aspects in the inner circle and secondary aspects in the outer circle, with a long-tail layout to visualize tail aspects. Zoom in for more detailed information.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To delve deeper into the underlying mechanisms, we selected the moderately-dense layer typology employed in software development, which serves as a representative case, with similar phenomena consistently occurring in other topologies and scenarios.
Specifically, we classified the aspects discussed in agents’ interactions into five main categories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh &amp; Oh, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kohn, 2019</a>)</cite>: four levels of errors (syntax, runtime, logic, and unmet requirements) and a non-error category; each category contains multiple subcategories.
Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 3.4 What Factors Might Contribute to Collaborative Emergence? ‣ 3 Evaluation ‣ Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Collaboration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> displays the total number of interaction aspects, along with their detailed distribution.
Within smaller topologies (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{0}\leq|\mathcal{V}|\leq 2^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{0}\leq|\mathcal{V}|\leq 2^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>), the limited interaction density confines aspects to approximately a dozen secondary aspects. However, as the network expands (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{4}\leq|\mathcal{V}|\leq 2^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{4}\leq|\mathcal{V}|\leq 2^{6}</annotation></semantics></math>), the interaction density increases quadratically, resulting in a sudden increase to dozens of aspects, followed by a more gradual rise.
This progression closely parallels the trend observed in emergent capabilities, which may partially attribute the emergence to the sharp rise in detailed interacted aspects among agents.
This phenomenon occurs because the token distribution from underlying models typically follows a long-tail pattern, necessitating larger-scale sampling to likely capture these tail tokens.
Consequently, this encourages the emergence of more infrequent "tail aspects", allowing the collaborative process to extend beyond the most common aspects.
Theoretically, the probability of a long-tail token <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> appearing at least once in <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> samples is:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

1-\left(1-1/r(t)\right)^{|\mathcal{V}|^{2}}\quad\lim_{|\mathcal{V}|\rightarrow\infty}p^{n}(t)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}p^{n}(t)=1" display="block" mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo 1-\left(1-1/r(t)\right)^{|\mathcal{V}|^{2}}\quad\lim_{|\mathcal{V}|\rightarrow\infty}p^{n}(t)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}p^{n}(t)=1</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t)\propto 1/r(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t)\propto 1/r(t)</annotation></semantics></math> represents a standard Zipf’s law characterizing a long-tailed distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Newman, 2005</a>)</cite>; the sampling size <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is proportional to the interaction density, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e., <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\propto|\mathcal{V}|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\propto|\mathcal{V}|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></span>. It can be inferred that increasing the network size significantly enhances the probability of tail token occurrences, gradually approaching an asymptote. This probability becomes an inevitable event once the sample size is sufficiently large.
Statistically, when a critic suggests a particular aspect, there is a 93.10% statistical likelihood that an actor will implement the recommended refinement rather than disregard it. The scaling up enables critics to pinpoint finer issues within artifacts, guiding actors to initiate corresponding refinements. Consequently, each round of dialogue in the collaborative process refines artifacts from different aspects, naturally elevating the probability of producing more nuanced artifacts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In response to multidimensional considerations, scaling agents accordingly prolongs the overall length of artifacts. For instance, the token length increased by 7.51 times when scaling from <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This characteristic, over small-scale networks, facilitates the integration of detailed requirements, performance optimization, and other advanced factors, potentially encompassing abilities that shorter artifacts cannot. This is mainly due to the graph’s naturally divergent and convergent topologies, which enable artifacts to porpagate for strength-aggregated refinement. Therefore, unlike majority voting, this paradigm fosters interdependent interaction and length-extended regeneration among diversified artifacts, thereby producing more comprehensive ones.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Large Language Models</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Trained on vast datasets through next token prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and capable of manipulating billions of parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Muennighoff et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, LLMs have become pivotal in natural language processing due to their seamless integration of extensive knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shanahan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brants et al., 2007</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
Central to this breakthrough is the neural scaling law, which posits that loss descends as a power law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
The principle underscores that scaling up language models can lead to emergent abilities—where performance experiences a sudden leap as the model scales <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schaeffer et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Autonomous Agents</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these advancements, LLMs possess inherent limitations in enclosed reasoning, driving further research to integrate advanced capabilities such as context-aware memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hua et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, tool use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, procedural planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and role playing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, thereby transforming fundamental LLMs into versatile autonomous agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Richards, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mei et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Along this line, multi-agent collaboration has proven beneficial in uniting the expertise of diverse agents for autonomous task-solving <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib105" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talebirad &amp; Nadiri, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, which has widely propelled progress across various domains such as software development <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, game playing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vinyals et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, personalized recommendation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, medical treatment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, financial marketing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, educational teaching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, scientific research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baek et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghafarollahi &amp; Buehler, 2024</a>)</cite> and embodied control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024f</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Technically, in contrast to straightforward majority voting where individuals act independently <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, collective emergence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Woolley et al., 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hopfield, 1982</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Watts &amp; Strogatz, 1998</a>)</cite> posits that effective collaboration should evolve into an integrated system that promotes interdependent interactions and thoughtful decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Piatti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
As such, recent studies differentiate agents into distinct expertise and encourage task-oriented interactions, forming a chained workflow to sequentially reach final artifacts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>. Subsequent research seeks to organize expert agents in a tree structure for hierarchical information propagation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024d</a>)</cite> or in a graph with predefined node and edge functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuge et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study explores the impact of scaling multi-agent collaboration by introducing <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MacNet</span>, a scalable framework that utilizes graphs to organize agents and orchestrate their reasoning for autonomous task solving.
Extensive evaluations reveal that it effectively supports collaboration among over a thousand agents, with irregular topologies outperforming regular ones.
We also identify a <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">collaborative scaling law</span>—the overall performance follows a logistic growth pattern as agents scale, with collaborative emergence occurring earlier than previously observed neural emergence.
We speculate this may be because scaling agents catalyzes their multidimensional considerations during interactive reflection and refinement, thereby producing more comprehensive artifacts.
However, our research also indicates that there are limits on the scaling horizon. By extrapolating traditional scaling from training to inference, we posit that agent collaboration could serve as a "shortcut" to bypass the need for resource-intensive retraining by employing inference-time procedural thinking.</p>
</div>
</section>
